notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Ecclesiastes 5, drawn from the sources I was able to reach within my tool limits:

---

## Ecclesiastes 5 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into three major sections: right conduct in worship (vv. 1–7), reflections on oppression and wealth (vv. 8–17), and the concluding counsel to enjoy life as God's gift (vv. 18–20). Gill summarises: "directions concerning the worship of God … concerning prayer … concerning vows … and, as an antidote against those vanities, the fear of God is proposed" ([Gill's Exposition – Ecclesiastes 5 intro](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Precept Austin outlines it as: A. Worship (5:1–7), B. Wayward (5:8–9), C. Wealth (5:10–17), D. Warrant (5:18–20) ([Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-5-commentary)).

---

### v. 1 — "Guard your steps when you go to the house of God…"

**The traditional reading:** "Guard your feet" is a Hebrew idiom for watching one's conduct. According to the NET Bible notes cited at Precept Austin, "'foot' is a metonymy for 'step,' and 'step' is a metonymy for 'action'" — meaning "be careful what you do" ([Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-5-commentary)). Gill explains the allusion to the priests washing their feet before entering the tabernacle (Exod. 30:19), signifying "purity and cleanness of the conversation of the true worshippers of God" ([Gill on Eccl 5:1](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). David Guzik (Enduring Word) paraphrases: "Walk prudently when you go to the house of God … show care and think about consequences when we come to meet God." He quotes Maclaren: "Fruitful and acceptable worship begins before it begins" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)).

"Draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools": The Hebrew *shama* means both to hear and to obey. Kidner (cited by Guzik) notes the echo of 1 Sam. 15:22 — "to obey is better than sacrifice" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Precept Austin explains that "the sacrifice of fools refers to external religious acts done without inner reverence, humility, or repentance. Fools practice religion and ritual, without repentance" ([Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-5-commentary)). The Pulpit Commentary (seen via search snippet) similarly interprets the "sacrifice of fools" as thoughtless, insincere offerings that lack the heart ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Sam Storms says Solomon's warning targets those who treated "sacrifice (worship) like magic. They thought blood and smoke (incense) were what God wanted. They forgot that spirit and heart were essential ingredients of true sacrifice" — referencing Ps. 51:16–17 ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)).

**Who are the "fools"?** Precept Austin notes the Hebrew *kesil* denotes "one who is dull and obstinate" and refers to a person's "chosen outlook, rather than his mental equipment" (citing Kidner's Proverbs commentary). The fool "does not engage in a pursuit of wisdom … manifests a spiritual, rather than mental, problem … enjoys his folly … has no reverence for truth" ([Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-5-commentary)). Gill adds: "they think they are doing well, and doing God good service, when they are doing ill; they know not truly the object of worship, nor the spiritual nature of it" ([Gill on Eccl 5:1](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)).

---

### v. 2 — "Do not be quick to speak … let your words be few."

All commentators connect this to prayer. The Pulpit Commentary says: "The warning is against hasty and thoughtless words in prayer, words that go from the lips with glib facility, but come not from the heart" and notes Jesus' parallel warning against "vain repetitions" in Matt. 6:7 ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Gill explains that "anything and everything that comes up into the mind should not be uttered before God … men should consider before they speak to the King of kings" ([Gill on Eccl 5:2](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Guzik adds the practical illustration: Elijah prayed "short and sweet" while the priests of Baal "prayed hard and long" — and God answered Elijah (1 Kings 18) ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). He also quotes Trapp: "it is not the labour of the lips, but the travail of the heart that prevails with God" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)).

The ground for brevity is theological: "God is in heaven and you are on earth." Storms says: "Prayers are prone to become magical when we lose sight of God's majesty" ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)). The Pulpit Commentary notes: "The infinite distance between God and man, illustrated by the contrast of earth and the illimitable heaven, is the ground of the admonition to reverence" ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)).

---

### v. 3 — "As a dream comes through many cares, so the speech of a fool comes with many words."

The Pulpit Commentary explains the comparison: "Cares and anxieties in business or other matters occasion disturbed sleep … and produce all kinds of sick fancies and imaginations." So too, "excess of words, especially in addresses to God, produces a fool's voice, i.e. foolish speech" ([BibleHub – Pulpit Commentary on Eccl 5:3](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/5-3.htm)). Gill gives the same sense: "as that comes through a multiplicity of business in the daytime … and this brings on dreams in the night season, which are confused and incoherent … and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words; either his voice in conversation … or his voice in prayer, being like a man's dream, confused, incoherent, and rambling" ([Gill on Eccl 5:3](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). JFB (Jamieson–Fausset–Brown) similarly notes: "As much 'business,' engrossing the mind, gives birth to incoherent 'dreams,' so many words, uttered inconsiderately in prayer, give birth to and betray 'a fool's speech'" ([BibleHub – JFB](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Guzik paraphrases: "Just as being too busy gives you nightmares, so being a fool makes you a blabbermouth" (Living Bible paraphrase) ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)).

---

### v. 4 — "When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it…"

All commentators anchor this in Deut. 23:21–23. The Pulpit Commentary states: "a vow once made becomes of the nature of an oath, and its non-performance is a sin and sacrilege, and incurs the punishment of false swearing" ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Gill notes that vows are "free and indifferent things, which persons may make or not; there is no precept for them in the word of God" — yet once made, they must be kept speedily ([Gill on Eccl 5:4](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Guzik identifies broken vows as "a commonly overlooked and unappreciated sin among God's people" and lists marks of those who honour God: they are not quick to vow, they are serious about fulfilling vows, and they regard broken vows as sins to be confessed ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Eaton (cited by Guzik) warns: "God does not take broken vows lightly. A broken vow may incur his judgment upon our endeavours" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)).

**Divergence on vows across traditions:** Gill, a Reformed Baptist, explicitly says vows "seem not so agreeable to the Gospel dispensation, having a tendency to ensnare the mind … and therefore it is better to abstain from them" ([Gill on Eccl 5:4](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). The Pulpit Commentary (Anglican-leaning) does not discourage vows but stresses that "there is no harm in not vowing" (Deut. 23:22) ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). This reflects a subtle difference: some Reformed/Puritan traditions are more cautious about voluntary vows, while Anglican and Catholic traditions retain a place for them. (I was unable to reach Catholic or Orthodox sources directly on this verse within tool limits.)

---

### v. 5 — "It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it."

Gill observes: "a vow is an arbitrary thing; a man is not bound to make it … but when he has once vowed, he is then brought under an obligation" — paralleling Acts 5:4 ([Gill on Eccl 5:5](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). The Pulpit Commentary adds that "frivolous excuses for the evasion of vows were very common" in Talmudic times and notes Jesus' rebukes in Matt. 5:33–37 and 23:16–22, plus Paul's reproof of vow-breaking widows in 1 Tim. 5:12 ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). The principle is unanimous among commentators: integrity before God is non-negotiable.

---

### v. 6 — "Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin … do not tell the messenger that your vow was a mistake."

**Who is the "messenger" (or "angel")?** This is a debated term. Gill surveys the options: some say angels in general (present as witnesses in worship, 1 Tim. 5:21); some say each person's guardian angel; some say Christ, the Angel of the Covenant; but Gill concludes "it is most probable the priest is intended, called the angel, or messenger, of the Lord of hosts, Malachi 2:7" — the priest before whom one might seek release from a vow ([Gill on Eccl 5:6](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Eaton (cited by Guzik) notes: "Hebrew draws no distinction between messenger and angel, so several interpretations are open to us here" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Dr. Constable also identifies "the messenger of God" as the priest, adding that pleading a vow was a mistake "would not excuse the vow-maker (cf. Deuteronomy 23:21–23)" ([StudyLight – Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-5.html)).

"Destroy the work of your hands": Gill says this means God may curse whatever the vow was made about — houses, fields, or cattle (cf. Lev. 27:28), so that "instead of its succeeding, is destroyed, and comes to nothing" ([Gill on Eccl 5:6](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Constable similarly: "God may destroy the work of his hands" ([StudyLight – Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-5.html)).

---

### v. 7 — "For as many dreams bring futility, so do many words. Therefore, fear God."

This verse serves as a summary of vv. 1–6. The Pulpit Commentary explains: "The popular religion, which made much of dreams and verbosity and vows, is vanity, and has in it nothing substantial or comforting" — then contrasts: "But fear thou God … the writer recalls men to the fear of the one true God" ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Precept Austin identifies "Fear God" as the eighth and summary imperative of the section, calling believers to "stand in awe of God" with "deep respect, awe-filled obedience, and recognition of God's holiness" ([Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-5-commentary)). Gill draws a contrast between the "multitude of dreams" (false prophets, enchantments) and the singular duty to fear the Lord, citing Jer. 23:28 ([Gill on Eccl 5:7](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Guzik quotes Clarke: "Most certainly, he that fears God need fear nothing else" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)).

---

### v. 8 — "If you see the oppression of the poor … do not be astonished…"

**Traditional reading:** The Preacher counsels realism. The Pulpit Commentary: "In political life there is little that is satisfactory; yet one must not surrender one's belief in a superintending Providence" ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Guzik: "The Preacher spoke realistically about life under the sun. There is much oppression and perversion of justice. It should surprise no one" — quoting Kidner: "For all his hatred of injustice, Qoheleth pins no hopes on utopian schemes or on revolution. He knows what is in man" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)).

"One official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them": Most commentators see two layers. The Pulpit Commentary notes the bureaucratic chain of accountability — each official is watched by the one above. But Gill reads the "higher" as God Himself: "he that is higher than the highest regardeth: that is, God, who is the most high in all the earth … he 'regards' all his people, his eyes are on them … he regards their oppressors, and their oppressions; and will, in his own time, deliver them" ([Gill on Eccl 5:8](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Gill also sees a Trinitarian hint in "there be higher than they" (plural), interpreting this as Father, Son, and Spirit — "Jehovah the Father is above men … Christ, the Son of the Highest, is higher than the kings of the earth … and the Holy Spirit is the power of the Highest" ([Gill on Eccl 5:8](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). Most other commentators, however, take "higher" as referring to the chain of earthly officials, not a direct reference to the Trinity.

---

### v. 9 — "The produce of the earth is taken by all; the king himself profits from the fields."

This verse is notoriously difficult. The Pulpit Commentary notes that some "connect this verse with what precedes" (seeing it as a mitigating thought about tyranny) and others "connect with the following verses" (as an introduction to the theme of wealth). It prefers the latter, explaining: "riches add little to the real happiness of the possessors" ([BibleHub – Ellicott](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ecclesiastes/5.htm) — via search snippet). Guzik reads it as an ironic observation: "everyone depends on what comes from the farmer's field – even the king. The Preacher seemed to delight in these ironies of life." He quotes Clarke: "God joins the head and feet together; for while the peasant is protected by the king … the king himself is dependent on the peasant." Trapp is quoted: "Rex agro servit, The king is a servant to the field" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Gill interprets it as commending agriculture: "the excellency of the praise of tilling the earth is above all things" — the king himself benefits from cultivated land ([Gill on Eccl 5:9](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)).

---

### v. 10 — "He who loves money is never satisfied by money…"

**Traditional reading:** Wealth cannot satisfy. Guzik: "Of all people, Solomon knew that the gathering of riches did not satisfy." He quotes Kidner: "If anything is worse than the addiction money brings, it is the emptiness it leaves. Man, with eternity in his heart, needs better nourishment than this" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Storms: "The love of wealth yields no lasting satisfaction" ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)). Gill says this dissuades "from covetousness, or an over love of riches; because they are unsatisfying" ([Gill intro](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)).

---

### v. 11 — "When good things increase, so do those who consume them…"

The traditional reading is that wealth attracts dependants and parasites. Guzik: "as one's net worth increased, so did one's expenses – and the expectation of others." He quotes Trapp's colourful language: "Servants, friends, flatterers, trencher-men, pensioners, and other hangbys that will flock to a rich man, as crows do to a dead carcase, not to defend, but to devour it" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Storms: "The increase of wealth breeds parasites" (cf. Prov. 19:6–7) ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)). The owner's only profit is "to behold them with his eyes" — a fleeting and empty enjoyment.

---

### v. 12 — "The sleep of the worker is sweet … but the abundance of the rich man permits him no sleep."

Guzik: "Solomon indulged an envy of the laboring man, who has so much less to worry about. The rich man has greater worries and less sleep" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Storms quotes Hubbard: "Insomnia is much more likely to occur in the fancy houses on the hilltops than in the small cottages in the valley" ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)).

---

### vv. 13–14 — "Wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner, or wealth lost in a failed venture…"

Guzik says this describes "those who keep their riches with an ungenerous, clenched fist" — it is "riches kept for their owner to his hurt." Deane (quoted by Guzik): "Rather, preserved by the possessor, hoarded and guarded, only to bring their lord added grief when by some reverse of fortune he loses them" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Eaton (also Guzik): "The riches were suddenly and catastrophically lost, whether in foolish gambling, in a misguided venture, or in a sudden reversal of circumstances" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Constable translates "bad investment" (v. 14) broadly: "any misfortune that results in the loss of wealth" ([StudyLight – Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Storms: "The hoarding of wealth can do harm" and "the loss of wealth can cause grief and sorrow" ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)).

---

### vv. 15–16 — "As a man came from his mother's womb, so he will depart again, naked…"

This echoes Job 1:21 and 1 Tim. 6:7. Guzik: "Man comes with nothing into the world and leaves the same way." He adds a New Testament application: "You can't take your wealth with you when you die; but you can send it on ahead by generous giving to God's work" — a reference to laying up treasure in heaven (Matt. 6:20) ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Constable: "Death itself is such a misfortune that overtakes everyone eventually and robs him of his wealth" ([StudyLight – Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-5.html)).

---

### v. 17 — "Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger."

Guzik calls this a sympathetic portrait of the lonely, sorrowful rich man: "With a sympathetic touch, Solomon tells us the loneliness, sorrow, and anger there is even for the very wealthy" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Constable says this verse "pictures the miserly workaholic. One example is Ebenezer Scrooge in Charles Dickens' *A Christmas Carol*" ([StudyLight – Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Storms: "The long term effects of wealth can be personally destructive" ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)).

---

### v. 18 — "Here is what I have seen to be good and fitting: to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor…"

This is the fourth "carpe diem" passage in Ecclesiastes (cf. 2:24–26; 3:12–13; 3:22). Constable: "Solomon was not advocating hedonism but the simple enjoyment of life day by day … Seize the day (Lat. carpe diem)! Smell the roses!" ([StudyLight – Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Guzik notes that Solomon says this "still very much with the premise of under the sun" — making the best of a bad situation ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). The Pulpit Commentary says this returns "to his old conclusion, that man should make the best of life, and enjoy all the good that God gives with moderation and contentment" ([StudyLight – Pulpit Commentary](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). The Expositor's Bible Commentary (via StudyLight) adds: "a quiet, cheerful, and obedient heart is greater riches than the wealthiest estate" ([StudyLight – Expositor's](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ecclesiastes-5.html)).

---

### v. 19 — "God has given riches and wealth to every man, and He has enabled him to enjoy them… This is a gift from God."

Guzik: "Though the Preacher knew that riches did not bring true meaning to life, he was no fool. He understood that it was better to have wealth than to not have it, and under the sun, one should enjoy both wealth and the capacity to enjoy it as the gift of God." He quotes Morgan: "Do not hoard anything, but enjoy it" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Storms: "Give thanks to God!" — the ability to enjoy wealth is itself a divine gift ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)). Desiring God (John Piper's ministry) references this verse in connection with Eccl. 11:7–8, calling it a call to "God-conscious joy" — "Taking pleasure in the things of earth as a gift of God is a means of divine grace, for the moments of delight keep us from being overwhelmed during the many days of darkness" ([Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ecclesiastes-finding-joy-amidst-lifes-enigmas)).

---

### v. 20 — "For a man seldom considers the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart."

Guzik: "This was Solomon's counsel to the wealthy man who finds no ultimate meaning under the sun. Simply, try not to think about it and keep yourself busy" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). The Expositor's Bible Commentary offers a richer reading: "He does not fret over the brevity of his life … for he knows that the joy his heart takes in the toils and pleasures of life is approved by God, or even … corresponds in some measure with the joy of God Himself; that his tranquil enjoyment is a reflection of the Divine peace" ([StudyLight – Expositor's](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ecclesiastes-5.html)). Desiring God notes that the phrase "God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart" means that God uses present joy to prevent excessive brooding over life's brevity and sorrows ([Desiring God](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ecclesiastes-finding-joy-amidst-lifes-enigmas)).

---

## Denominational Distinctives & Other Views

### Broad agreement across traditions

On Ecclesiastes 5, the major Protestant traditions are substantially in agreement on the plain sense: worship requires reverence, vows must be kept, wealth is ultimately unsatisfying, and enjoyment of life is God's gift. The differences are matters of emphasis, not contradiction.

### Baptist

Gill (Reformed Baptist) emphasises that vows under the New Covenant "seem not so agreeable to the Gospel dispensation" and it is "better to abstain from them" — reflecting the free-church wariness of binding religious vows beyond those commanded in Scripture ([Gill on Eccl 5:4](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ecclesiastes/5.htm)). The Bridgeway Bible Commentary (Baptist-leaning) emphasises the practical warning: "the offering of sacrifices is useless if the worshippers have no desire to listen to God's word or obey it" ([StudyLight – Bridgeway](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ecclesiastes-5.html)).

### Pentecostal/Charismatic

David Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic) and Sam Storms (charismatic-Reformed) focus on the heart of worship. Guzik's application is pastoral and devotional — he warns against "the sin of broken vows – promising things to God and failing to live up to the vow" as "commonly overlooked" ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ecclesiastes-5/)). Storms frames the worship section as a warning against letting life's perplexities breed "practical atheism" and "sloppy spirituality" ([Sam Storms](https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/ecclesiastes-5:1-20)).

### Reformed

Reformed commentators (like Dr. Constable at Dallas Theological Seminary, dispensational-Reformed) emphasise the "under the sun" framework, seeing the chapter as demonstrating "the ultimate futility of human achievement" (the ninth and final occurrence of "striving after wind" closes this section at 6:9) ([StudyLight – Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ecclesiastes-5.html)). The Precept Austin commentary (broadly Reformed-evangelical) gives meticulous attention to Hebrew grammar, identifying eight imperatives/jussives in vv. 1–7 that structure the passage ([Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-5-commentary)).

### Lutheran

I was unable to reach specific Lutheran commentaries (lcms.org, 1517.org) within my tool limits for this chapter.

### Methodist/Wesleyan

I was unable to reach specific Wesleyan/Methodist sources (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) within my tool limits.

### Catholic and Orthodox

I was unable to reach Catholic sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox sources (oca.org) within my tool limits. The Catholic interpretative tradition on this passage (drawing from the Vulgate and Church Fathers) would likely note that v. 1 in the Vulgate reads, "Keep thy foot, when thou goest into the house of God, and draw nigh to hear" — with the traditional Catholic emphasis on the reverent participation in the liturgy and the binding nature of religious vows (including monastic and marriage vows). St. Gregory the Great's comment on dreams (cited in the Pulpit Commentary) is noted: "Sometimes dreams are engendered of fullness or emptiness of the belly, sometimes of illusion, sometimes of illusion and thought combined, sometimes of revelation" ([BibleHub – Pulpit Commentary on Eccl 5:3](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ecclesiastes/5-3.htm)). But fuller Catholic and Orthodox resources were beyond my reach.

### Modern Scholarship

The NET Bible notes (cited at Precept Austin) clarify the textual issue in v. 1: the Hebrew text (BHS) verse numbering differs from English Bibles — Eccl. 5:1 ET = 4:17 HT, and this offset continues through the chapter ([Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-5-commentary)). The NET also notes the idiom "Guard your feet" is a compound metonymy for "Be careful what you do." These notes also clarify that "draw near to listen" (*lishmoa*) may be taken literally ("to listen" in contrast to speak) or figuratively ("to obey"), with the context favouring "to listen" because the section warns against rash vows and hasty speech ([Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/ecclesiastes-5-commentary)). I was unable to access bibleodyssey.org directly for this chapter.
